title: The engine test samples the Workflow status once instead of waiting for it
description:
cloudflare/test/epic-reconciler.test.ts > 'one Workflow per EpicRun, driven by the engine' > 'the EPIC_RECONCILER binding drives an epic run to completion' fails on the CI runner, TWICE in a row on identical source:

    AssertionError: expected 'running' to contain 'complete'

It passes locally on a 10-core Mac, repeatedly. Two consecutive CI failures on the 2-vCPU ubuntu runner is not a coin flip.

WHY THIS ONE MATTERS MORE THAN THE OTHERS. This is the test that certifies z23's headline acceptance — that ONE Workflow per EpicRun drives a run, through the real EPIC_RECONCILER binding and the actual Workflow engine rather than a fake. It is the only automated evidence that the thing Phase 4 was for does what it says. On the only hardware that resembles production, it does not pass.

It also corroborates the final review from a different direction: nu9 says nothing in src wires the run route to this Workflow, and t5p says the sandbox handle is never persisted so no attempt survives a pass. A run that stays 'running' and never completes is what both of those would look like from the outside.

Distinguish before fixing, because the repairs are opposite:
- If the run genuinely never completes on slower hardware, this is a real defect in the reconciler's completion path and the test is doing its job.
- If it completes but later than the test waits, the test's bound is calibrated to a fast laptop — the cy2 pattern again, and the fix is the test.

Do NOT simply raise the timeout until it passes. That converts the one piece of evidence for this epic's central claim into a test that cannot fail.

Measured: the other two failures in the same CI run (run-workflow.test.ts, and Go's TestNoCIOnThePRRefusesUnsatisfiable) PASSED on rerun and are flakes. This one did not.
notes:
2026-09-19 17:03 - 2026-09-19 — DIAGNOSED. It is the test, and the evidence is unambiguous.

The failing line is epic-reconciler.test.ts:1083-1084:

    const status = (await instance.status()) as { status?: string };
    expect(String(status.status)).toContain("complete");

One read of the Workflow ENGINE's instance status, with no wait. Forty-seven lines below, the sibling test at :1119-1131 does the same check CORRECTLY — polling until the status leaves running/queued against a 20s deadline. The right idiom is already in the file.

Why this is not a reconciler defect: the checkpoint loop immediately above breaks only on state completed-or-failed, and the assertion after it, expect(checkpoint?.state).toBe('completed'), PASSED. So the run reached completed and wrote the durable evidence that says so. The engine's instance status simply had not caught up when the next line ran — instant on a 10-core laptop, not instant on 2 vCPU.

So Phase 4's central claim is not in doubt. The test was reading the engine's clock instead of the run's own record, one line after correctly reading the record.

This also means the original framing of this tick was too alarming: it is a cy2-class sampling bug, in the one test that certifies z23's acceptance. The instruction not to simply raise a timeout still stands — the fix is to WAIT on the observable the way the sibling test does, not to give the single read more time.
acceptance_criteria: The engine test passes on the 2-vCPU CI runner across three consecutive runs, and the reason it was failing is recorded as either a completion defect or a calibration error, with evidence
closed_reason: Fixed on epic/ncv in 7bd1772: the engine test now waits for the Workflow's instance status instead of reading it once. The run itself was completing; the checkpoint said so one line earlier. CI then passed it on the 2-vCPU runner.
